title: Crossing the ocean
hookLine: the world is an ocean hard to cross; Nanak says attention on the Word carries you over

lines: THE DUCK WAS HALF THE ANSWER.
cards: Dutar. Hard to cross. That's how the yogi Charpat describes the world when he puts his question to Nanak, near the start of the Sidh Gosht.
The world is an ocean, he says, and they call it hard to cross. How does anyone reach the far shore? Six days ago came half the answer, the duck that swims the stream and stays dry.
But the duck was only the first move, and the stanza doesn't leave Charpat in the water.

teach.b: The rest of the stanza, in paraphrase: with attention fixed on the Word, the terrifying world-ocean is crossed by speaking the Name. The phrase for the world-ocean is bhav saagar. Saagar is the sea.
Bhav is the world of becoming, the churn of being born, wanting, losing, wanting again.
Nanak accepts the yogi's picture. He doesn't say the world is a calm pond or that Charpat exaggerates. The water really is deep, and the waves are real.
What he changes is the way across. One way is to climb above the water, onto a peak the waves can't reach.
Nanak's answer goes through it: attention resting on the Word holds a person up while they cross. Elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru and the Name are pictured as a boat or a ship.
The world is the ocean; the Word is the boat. And the picture is honest.

teach.h: THE BOAT DOESN'T SHRINK THE SEA.
teach.b: A boat doesn't make the sea smaller. The storm still comes, and you still get wet.
But a person in a boat isn't fighting the water with their own arms; they're held by something built for the crossing. Yesterday, attention tuned to the Word was the disciple.
Today, it's how the disciple crosses: learning, and staying afloat. On a bad night, one line, held, may be all a person has, and in this stanza it carries someone over.

how: Sikhs speak of the world as bhav saagar, the world-ocean, and of the Guru's Word and the Name as what carries a person across; the image returns in Gurbani sung in kirtan.

o: a yogic breath practice for swimming through cold water
Nanak to Charpat: attention on the Word carries you
a song sailors sang when setting out across the sea

games.q: what's inside the crossing — tap the pairs.

s: Nanak tells Charpat the world is really a calm pond
he accepts the deep water; he changes the way across.
in the stanza, attention fixed on the Word crosses the world-ocean
with attention on the Word, the world-ocean is crossed by speaking the Name.
the way across, in this answer, is to climb above the water
the answer goes through the water, held up by the Word.

games.q: you're in deep water and the far shore is a long way off. Charpat asks how anyone crosses. what does the stanza say carries you?
o: swimming harder on your own strength.
waiting on the shore until the sea is calm.
games.why: with attention on the Word, the world-ocean is crossed, says the stanza, by speaking the Name.

practice: Let your eyes rest on some water, a glass on the table, rain on a window, or just the memory of a lake, and let the breath come and go like small waves.

Bring to mind one thing that feels deep or rough right now, and without trying to calm it, picture yourself held above it, giving your attention one line to rest on: Waheguru, or today's line, the word is the boat.
If you pray, let that line carry the weight for a while.

wordCard.voice: Crossing the ocean. Charpat's question about the world-ocean, hard to cross, and Nanak's answer: with attention on the Word, a person crosses over. Today's word.

orig.note: saagar: the sea; with bhav, the world-ocean Charpat calls hard to cross.

carryVoice: Your line: the word is the boat. It doesn't shrink the sea; it carries you across. Thanks for sitting with me today.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 4–5, Ang 938 (Charpat's question; surat sabad bhav saagar tareeai)
